title: Truncated Wigner dynamics of biclique quantum spin glasses
abstract: Quantum spin glasses are often considered testbeds for studying quantum optimization algorithms and as such have been the subject of various quantum advantage claims. Here we investigate the near adiabatic dynamics of biclique quantum spin glasses within the (discrete) truncated Wigner approximation (TWA). Benchmarks on small systems show that TWA recovers sample-to-sample fluctuations of the Edwards-Anderson order parameter, over a wide range of annealing times, with increasing fidelity when the system size increases. We extract critical exponents from the Binder cumulant in line with theoretical expectations, reproducing recent quantum experiments. The computational cost of the method is minimal and it can easily be applied to tens of thousands of qubits.
summary: This paper analyzes the non-equilibrium dynamics of biclique quantum spin glasses using the Truncated Wigner Approximation (TWA). The authors demonstrate that TWA accurately captures crucial physical signatures, such as sample fluctuations and critical exponents, across large system sizes. This validates TWA as a powerful, scalable tool for studying quantum phase transitions in disordered magnetic systems.
main_problem: The study investigates how accurately the Truncated Wigner Approximation (TWA) captures the near adiabatic dynamics of biclique quantum spin glasses, particularly concerning sample-to-sample fluctuations.
main_result: TWA successfully recovers sample-to-sample fluctuations of the Edwards-Anderson order parameter and extracts critical exponents consistent with theoretical expectations across increasing system sizes.
method: The authors use the Truncated Wigner Approximation (TWA), a semiclassical method, to simulate the time evolution of the quantum spin glass Hamiltonian using Trotterization.
model_or_system: The physical system is a biclique quantum spin glass modeled by a time-dependent Ising Hamiltonian: H(t) = J(t/ta)H_0 + g(t/ta)H_x, involving $\sigma^z$ and $\sigma^x$ terms.
key_observables: Edwards-Anderson order parameter ($\langle q^2 angle$), Binder cumulant ($U$), and critical exponents ($\mu$, $r$).
important_parameters: Annealing time range, system size (up to tens of thousands of qubits), and the fidelity/correlation coefficient ($ho$) between TWA and exact results.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the TWA remains accurate in the large-N limit; discrepancies are noted at late times or for small systems with large order parameters.
figures_summary: Figures compare TWA to exact simulations, showing good agreement ($ho > 99\%$) and demonstrating data collapse of the Binder cumulant consistent with theoretical predictions across varying system sizes.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem by introducing the model and method (TWA). It then presents results showing that TWA captures key non-equilibrium features, such as sample fluctuations and critical exponents, validating its use for studying quantum phase transitions in spin glasses.
why_interesting: It provides a computationally inexpensive yet accurate semiclassical tool (TWA) to study complex many-body dynamics in disordered systems, which is relevant for understanding quantum criticality beyond mean-field treatments.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Quantum annealing schedule, with transverse ﬁeld g(t/ta) and overall Ising coupling J(t/ta), for an annealing time of ta = 1ns. The schedule is used in D-wave’s quantum annealing experiment [3]. The inset shows a K4,4 biclique graph.

FIG. 2. Spin glass order parameter for (from left to right) biclique graphs K4,4, K6,6 and K8,8. The solid lines show the exact result obtained using full state vector simulations with the same Trotterization, while the dots denote the truncated Wigner results. Diﬀerent colors indicate diﬀerent annealing times ta going from ta = 4ns (dark green) to ta = 25ns (yellow).

FIG. 3. The Pearson correlation coeﬃcient ρ between the TWA and exact ⟨ q2⟩ is extracted from a population of Ns = 100 diﬀerent biclique graphs. As measure of inﬁdelity, the main ﬁgure shows 1−ρ, as a function of annealing time ta, for diﬀerent system sizes K4,4, K6,6 and K8,8. This inset shows a scatter plot for K8,8, and is simply a diﬀerent representation of the data in Fig. 2; it can be directly compared to Ref. [3].

FIG. 4. The main ﬁgure shows the Binder cumulant U ex- tracted as a function of rescaled time, for systems ranging from K8,8 (yellow) to K32,32 (blue) (increasing each subset by 4 qubits) and times ranging from ta = 7ns to ta = 40ns.
